chapter: Los Angeles 1947-48, Rock Island and bebop in New York
title: Jail, the courtroom crowd and the guilty fine
summary: They were put on display in court, fined over $200 and photographed.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: When we get back there in jail, all of the cells was empty. So there was no need for any of them to be locked. So we're just walking in and around, you know, just walking the floors, pacing. Ike is sitting down in one of the cells, nursing his head, trying to stop it from bleeding, with toilet tissue, yet. So we were there I guess about 10 or 15 minutes, and our names were called. We stepped up to this little peephole, a glass window, I guess about a foot wide and about a half a foot tall, just a peephole, you know. So the fellow said, "We brought a -- these fellows wanted to see the one that looks like an Arab." Well, naturally, that was me and my beard and my mouth, you know. So after they had left, about 10 minutes after that, they called our names again. But this time we were ushered out another door. And when we looked up, we were in the courtroom, in a little box, where we're all squeezed real tightly. It wasn't even a fit where we could sit comfortably, you know. It was like sardines in a can, and we was all together. Ike's trying to pat his head. Charlie's skin is oily, and he's trying to get some oil off of his skin, where he'd been up all night. My skin was oily. I was doing likewise. I mean, who were we going to impress even if our skin wasn't oily? You know. The papers had released that we were resisting arrest, disorderly conduct, drunk.
I thought you said you'd been in there 15 minutes.
I thought you said you'd been in the cell 15 minutes.
Yeah. But the Judge read off the charges and this was in the newspapers, and the courtroom was full of onlookers. They come in --
Well, how long were you in jail?

Well, it was early in the morning, you know. See, we had played that night and gotten off from work, and then we went through this thing at the station, and then being booked and being put in the cells. We weren't in there any time before the Court opened, you know? Broad daylight. As soon as day hit, the Court opened, because the newspapers hit the streets early and everyone had read it. They were there to see the three people that was going to be in the box, you know. A show. A little excitement for the town, you know. We shook the town up and the town shook us up. So he said, 'How do you plead.' I speak up right away. 'Not guilty.' Charlie doesn't say anything. Ike said, 'Man, come on, let's get out of here, whatever it costs us.' I said, 'Well, Ike if you plead guilty, you don't have any comeback with the NAACP in Chicago or the Urban League, they can't fight the case because you said guilty.' 'Man, no, I might have as much sense as you if I don't try.' He said, 'Let's get out of here.' The Judge said, 'Well, the fine will be --', two hundred and some odd dollars.
